text: The oldest way to make fire is to rub two sticks together. But it takes so long that your arms give out.
So people made chemical matches that burst into flame when you dipped them in acid. But then you had to carry a bottle of acid around.
Next came matches that you dragged through sandpaper. But they stank of sulfur, and burning bits fell onto the carpet.
So match makers switched to white phosphorus, which lit on anything you struck it against. But it lit so easily that it had to be kept in a sealed tin.
Worse, it was poison. The fumes destroyed the jawbones of the factory workers, and their bones even glowed in the dark.
So match makers split the match in two. The head got one set of chemicals, and the strip on the box got red phosphorus.
Neither half can catch fire on its own. They only light when you rub them together. That is why it is called a safety match.
So striking a match still works like the very first fire. You are rubbing two things together, with some chemical help!
